content: Yoga, derived from the Sanskrit term yuj, meaning to control, to yoke, or to unite, refers to a collection of ancient spiritual practices originating in India. These practices are designed to achieve spiritual insight, self-discipline, and a profound understanding of existence. According to Gavin Flood, an academic authority on Hindu studies, yoga encompasses techniques of asceticism and meditation that aim to foster spiritual experiences and deep comprehension of the nature of reality. While yoga is deeply rooted in Indian religious traditions, including Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism, its global perception often focuses on the physical postures (asanas) of Hatha Yoga or its use as a form of exercise. The philosophical and practical aspects of yoga are extensively discussed in classical Indian texts such as the Upanishads, the Bhagavad Gita, the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali, the Hatha Yoga Pradipika, and the Shiva Samhita. Yoga is traditionally categorized into major branches, including Hatha Yoga (focused on physical postures and breath control), Karma Yoga (the yoga of action), Jnana Yoga (the yoga of knowledge), Bhakti Yoga (the yoga of devotion), and Raja Yoga (the yoga of mental discipline and meditation). Raja Yoga, as outlined in the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali, is one of the six orthodox schools of Hindu philosophy and emphasizes the control of the mind to achieve spiritual liberation. Historical Origins of Yoga Evidence of yoga-like practices dates back to the Indus Valley Civilization (circa 3300–1700 BCE). Archaeological findings, such as seals depicting figures in meditative postures, suggest that ritual discipline and concentration were integral to the culture. The Pashupati seal, discovered by John Marshall, has been interpreted by some as representing a proto-Shiva figure in a yogic pose, though this interpretation remains speculative. Scholars like Jonathan Mark Kenoyer and Heinrich Zimmer support the idea that these artifacts reflect early forms of yoga. Literary Foundations of Yoga The earliest references to ascetic practices (tapas) and meditation appear in the Vedic texts (900–500 BCE) and the Upanishads. The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, one of the oldest Upanishads, mentions meditation as a spiritual practice. The Bhagavad Gita, a key text within the Mahabharata, extensively discusses yoga in various forms, emphasizing Karma Yoga (selfless action), Bhakti Yoga (devotion), and Jnana Yoga (knowledge). Commentators like Madhusudana Sarasvati have divided the Gita into sections corresponding to these three yogic paths. The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali, composed between 100 BCE and 500 CE, provide a systematic framework for yoga philosophy and practice. Patanjali defines yoga as the cessation of mental fluctuations (citta vritti nirodha) and outlines an eight-limbed path (Ashtanga Yoga) that includes ethical principles (yamas and niyamas), physical postures (asanas), breath control (pranayama), sensory withdrawal (pratyahara), concentration (dharana), meditation (dhyana), and ultimate absorption (samadhi). This system emphasizes mental discipline and spiritual liberation (kaivalya). Hatha Yoga and Its Evolution Hatha Yoga, as described in the 15th-century text Hatha Yoga Pradipika by Yogi Swatmarama, focuses on the purification of the body (shatkarma) as a means to purify the mind and vital energy (prana). Unlike Raja Yoga, which begins with mental and spiritual purification, Hatha Yoga emphasizes physical postures and breath control. It incorporates tantric elements, including the concepts of chakras and kundalini energy. Modern Hatha Yoga, often associated with physical fitness, has become the most widely recognized form of yoga in the West, though it represents only one aspect of the broader yogic tradition. Yoga in Buddhism and Tantra Yoga has significantly influenced Buddhist practices, particularly in the development of meditation techniques and spiritual exercises. The Yogacara school of Mahayana Buddhism, established in the 4th to 5th centuries, integrates yogic principles into its framework for achieving enlightenment. Zen Buddhism, derived from the Sanskrit term dhyana (meditation), shares similarities with yogic practices, emphasizing mindfulness and meditative absorption. Tibetan Buddhism incorporates advanced yogic techniques, such as Mahayoga, Anuyoga, and Atiyoga, as well as physical postures and breath control (Trul khor) to harmonize body and mind. Tantric traditions also incorporate yoga as a means of transcending ordinary reality and achieving liberation. Tantric practices often involve meditation on chakras and kundalini energy, aiming to awaken spiritual consciousness and unite the individual with the divine. Goals of Yoga The ultimate goal of yoga varies across traditions. In Advaita Vedanta and Shaivism, the aim is Moksha, or liberation from the cycle of birth and death (samsara), achieved through the realization of oneness with the Supreme Brahman. In Bhakti traditions, the goal is an eternal relationship with a personal deity, such as Vishnu or Krishna. For many modern practitioners, yoga serves as a means to improve physical health, mental clarity, and overall well-being, though its spiritual dimensions remain central to its traditional purpose.
